rv.q: It not only absolves the Victorian era of its sins of excess, it carries its charms lightly, to ensure that grace does indeed pervade.
Raison gives a performance of impish, provoking vivacity but is rarely required to be anything more than a foil and a feed – and possibly a lover - to Irving.
Hare’s play becomes a sweet panegyric, and a really traditional, really entertaining night both at the theatre and of the theatre.
Hare doesn't let his audience love it too, because he's too obsessed with overlaying it with his own agenda of old (good) versus new (diabolical).
Together, they anchor a play that is by turns wickedly funny, surprisingly moving, and endlessly fascinating for anyone with even a passing love of theatre.
The acting across the board is superb, including from, of course, the famously talented Fiennes.
Grace Pervades, Hare's 32nd play, is in many ways unexpected, an insight into a semi-forgotten time.
This is an informative and amusing comedy, a little arid in parts, which students of theatrical history will adore.

David Hare’s musings on actors and acting — and in particular the personal and professional relationship which developed between two of the greatest exponents of stage craft, provides an interesting biographical insight, albeit not the playwright's best work.
The script is intelligent and often very funny, but also there are some slow-moving sections to the dialogue, which occasionally comes across as clunky.
Ralph Fiennes and Miranda Raison are beautifully paired as the couple.

The result allows the golden-throated Fiennes to dip into a Shakespeare repertoire which no one of his generation knows as well as he, while allowing a shining-faced Raison to hold her own, and then some.
This can't miss production is strong in its staging, writing, and direction, and pulls smashing performances from its brilliant cast.
This fine work will appeal to the widest possible range of audiences but is a joy for anybody in the business or enamoured of theatre history.
Grace Pervades is a lovely, well-balanced show, taking the interesting stories that happened just off stage and putting them on stage – in the most complimentary way possible.

cn.t: Fiennes and Raison deliver outstanding performances in Hare's affectionate love letter to Victorian theatre legends Irving and Terry, though critics are divided on whether the play itself matches its stars' brilliance.
